extracted.intended_audience: press officers, science communicators, and journalists producing or evaluating science press releases
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluation checklist for producing and critiquing evidence-based science press releases so media coverage accurately represents study findings. Includes checklists for press officers and recommendations for journalists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate representation of the underlying study
rubrics_metrics.description: The release should accurately represent the study's aims, scope, population, and findings rather than overstating them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid hype that exceeds the study's findings; ensure headline, lede and conclusions reflect what the study actually shows. Cross-check release text against study text and data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodology summary provided
rubrics_metrics.description: A clear methodology summary should be included so readers (and journalists) can understand how the study was done.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the methods understandable to non-specialists while including key elements (design, sample size, endpoints, major analyses). Use the critique question 'Is methodology clear?' when evaluating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations explicitly stated
rubrics_metrics.description: State the study's limitations clearly in the release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not omit limitations. Journalists are advised to note limitations in their articles. Missing limitations is a common problem tracked by SMC and undermines accurate reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect sizes given in both relative and absolute terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Statistical effects should be reported fully — include both relative and absolute effect sizes, not relative-only framing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid obscuring effect magnitude by only giving percentages or rate ratios. Provide baseline rates when presenting rate ratios so readers can understand practical significance (addresses 'Rate ratios without baseline rates' issue).

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple expert voices included
rubrics_metrics.description: Include multiple expert voices, not just authors, to provide external context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide external commentary from non-author scientists and include external expert quotes. Avoid a single-author voice without external context; SMC recommends including external expert quotes and commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: External commentary from non-author scientists / External expert quotes included
rubrics_metrics.description: Cite or quote independent experts who can contextualise and critique the findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer quotes from independent scientists rather than only authors. This helps guard against one-sided claims and provides balanced interpretation for journalists and the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline matches the study
rubrics_metrics.description: The press release headline should accurately reflect the study findings and not overclaim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SMC analysts ask 'Does the headline match the study?' when critiquing releases. Avoid headline hype that wasn't in the release or the paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lede is accurate
rubrics_metrics.description: The leading paragraph (lede) of the release should accurately summarise the central finding without exaggeration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SMC's critique format specifically evaluates whether 'the lede is accurate.' Ensure the lede does not omit key caveats or overstate causality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclusions appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Conclusions and implied claims must be supported by the study's design and results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SMC asks 'Are the conclusions appropriate?' Avoid drawing causal inferences from correlational data or treating exploratory/subgroup findings as definitive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid causal language for correlational findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use causal wording to describe associations found in observational or correlational studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify causal claims with a statistician; explicitly label associations as correlational. 'Correlations described as causes' is a common misuse flagged by SMC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid hype that exceeds the study's findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not overstate significance, clinical relevance, or broader implications beyond what the data support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid framing preclinical or early-stage research as therapeutically ready, and avoid calling findings 'breakthrough' or 'revolutionary' without verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not over-extrapolate animal or preclinical work to humans
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid presenting animal or preclinical findings as directly human-relevant or therapeutic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SMC tracks 'animal studies framed as human-relevant' and 'preclinical work hyped as therapeutic' as frequent problems. Make translational limits explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not treat subgroup analyses as primary findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid presenting subgroup or post-hoc analyses as if they were primary, pre-specified findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag subgroup analyses and interpret them cautiously; state whether analyses were pre-specified and note limitations of reduced power or multiplicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide baseline rates when using rate ratios
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting rate ratios or relative risks, also give baseline rates so absolute impact is clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This addresses the 'Rate ratios without baseline rates' anti-pattern and helps readers assess practical significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unverified 'first'/'breakthrough'/'revolutionary' claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use superlative language such as 'first', 'breakthrough', or 'revolutionary' unless independently verified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SMC explicitly lists these terms as problematic when used without verification; verify claims of novelty or primacy with literature checks or editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclose all funding sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Funding sources and conflicts of interest should be disclosed in the release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SMC recommends disclosing all funding sources as part of transparent communication; omission can mislead journalists and readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify embargo time clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: Clearly state any embargo time and embargo conditions in the release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SMC's recommendations for press officers include specifying embargo time clearly to avoid confusion and ensure coordinated reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have authors review the release before issue
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should review press release drafts prior to distribution to ensure accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SMC recommends authors review releases to catch inaccuracies; this is part of best practice for press officers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Run drafts past a statistical reviewer
rubrics_metrics.description: Have a statistical reviewer check drafts for appropriate representation of analyses and claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SMC recommends running drafts past a statistical reviewer to avoid misrepresentation of methods, results, or causal claims and to ensure effect sizes are presented correctly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalists: read the underlying paper before writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists should read the full study before reporting to verify claims and understand limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of SMC's advice to journalists: reading the paper helps avoid repeating press-release hype and lets reporters verify methodology, results, and limitations.
